section_summary: This section begins with U.S. diplomatic reporting and cross-references concerning suspected Japanese military, aviation, immigration, landholding, commercial, religious, and cultural activities in Brazil between 1934 and 1938. It then documents Japanese propaganda distributed in Brazil, including a leaflet defending Japan's conduct in the Sino-Japanese War and the first sixty pages of a much longer illustrated booklet, Japan-China Pictorial Primer: Do You Know That...?, presenting an extensive anti-Chinese and anti-Communist justification of Japanese policy. Brazilian officials generally had no concrete evidence of covert Japanese military preparations but nevertheless investigated Japanese settlements, landed holdings, and possible airfields.

subfiles.title: Cross-reference sheet: Japanese activities in Brazil and a proposed Amazon republic
subfiles.about: The sheet directs readers to another file concerning claims that Japanese officers might try to establish a Japanese-controlled republic in the Amazon.
subfiles.summary: This filing note cross-references document 832.61334/16. It characterizes the referenced report as a discussion of Japanese activities in Brazil and speculation that the Japanese involved might be military officers seeking control of an Amazon republic.

subfiles.title: Summary of Rio de Janeiro despatch No. 608
subfiles.from: Department of State, Division of Far Eastern Affairs
subfiles.about: The memorandum summarizes Brazilian inquiries into possible Japanese air bases and expectations concerning a forthcoming Japanese commercial mission.
subfiles.summary: The Brazilian Foreign Minister had ordered investigations in Amazonas and Pará but disclosed no concrete basis for suspecting Japanese air-base construction. He expected the Japanese Commercial Mission to seek a higher immigration quota and increased cotton purchases, while doubting that either effort would produce major results.

subfiles.title: Despatch No. 608: Potential Japanese Activities in Brazil
subfiles.from: George A. Gordon, U.S. Chargé d'Affaires ad interim, Rio de Janeiro
subfiles.about: The despatch reports confidential remarks by Brazil's foreign minister about investigations of possible Japanese aviation preparations and the purposes of a Japanese commercial mission.
subfiles.summary: The Brazilian Foreign Minister said he had instructed the interventors of Amazonas and Pará to investigate any preparations for Japanese air bases, although he cited no concrete evidence. He described Japan as an unknown quantity requiring precaution. He also predicted that the forthcoming commercial mission might seek increased immigration and Brazilian cotton purchases, but considered major concessions or commercial agreements unlikely.

subfiles.title: Division of Far Eastern Affairs note concerning the drafting of a despatch
subfiles.from: Department of State, Division of Far Eastern Affairs
subfiles.about: A brief handwritten note records information that Theodore A. Xanthaky apparently drafted the related despatch.
subfiles.summary: The page is a short internal annotation rather than a substantive report. It identifies Xanthaky as the apparent drafter of the despatch under review.

subfiles.title: Despatch No. 805: Survey of Japanese Landed Holdings in Brazil
subfiles.from: Wesley Frost, U.S. Chargé d'Affaires ad interim, Rio de Janeiro
subfiles.about: The despatch forwards a memorandum about Brazil's confidential survey of Japanese activities and landholdings.
subfiles.summary: Frost encloses the record of an October 2 conversation between Foreign Minister José Carlos de Macedo Soares and Theodore A. Xanthaky. The survey was intended to determine the nature and extent of Japanese activities and landed property in Brazil.

subfiles.title: Memorandum of conversation with Foreign Minister Macedo Soares
subfiles.about: The memorandum records Brazil's nationwide inquiry into Japanese-owned land, possible landing fields, and other potentially military features.
subfiles.summary: Macedo Soares said Brazil's state governors were cooperating in a survey of all Japanese residents' activities and landed holdings, with special attention to landing fields and other military possibilities. He denied having evidence of suspicious conduct but argued that Japan's dispersed settlements, including those in the remote Amazon valley, warranted precaution. He agreed that the results could be shared with the United States as part of Brazil's policy of close political relations.

subfiles.title: Cross-reference sheet: Japanese commission and petroleum development in Bahia
subfiles.about: The sheet refers to a report on a Japanese commission's visit to Bahia and a proposed Japanese-financed petroleum company.
subfiles.summary: The note cross-references Bahia despatch No. 140. It identifies Oscar Cordeiro as planning to form a company with Japanese capital to exploit petroleum deposits after a Japanese commission visited the Bolsa de Mercadorias da Bahia.

subfiles.title: Despatch No. 1491: Japanese Propaganda in Brazil
subfiles.from: R. M. Scotten, Counselor of Embassy, for the Ambassador
subfiles.about: The despatch transmits Japanese propaganda publications concerning the Sino-Japanese War that were being distributed in Brazil.
subfiles.summary: Scotten forwards an English-language leaflet issued by the Foreign Affairs Association of Japan and a Portuguese pamphlet issued by the Nippon-Brasileira Association of Kobe. Both were being distributed through the Japanese Embassy in Brazil to justify Japan's conduct in China.

subfiles.title: Why? Who? How? Questions and Answers on the Sino-Japanese Conflict
subfiles.about: The leaflet presents twenty questions and answers defending Japanese military action in China.
subfiles.summary: The publication blames China for beginning hostilities, portrays Japanese troop deployments and bombing as defensive and lawful, and denies deliberate attacks on civilians. It argues that Chinese Communism threatens Japan, foreign interests, and the Pacific balance of power, while presenting Japan's war aims as cooperation rather than territorial conquest. A map of northern and central China and Tokyo publication details conclude the leaflet.

subfiles.title: Despatch on Brazilian cultural visitors to Japan
subfiles.from: R. M. Scotten, Counselor of Embassy, for the Ambassador
subfiles.about: The despatch reports Japanese sponsorship of Brazilian students as a form of foreign-government propaganda.
subfiles.summary: Aires de Azevedo was scheduled to leave Rio de Janeiro for two years of study in Japanese literature at Tokyo universities. His trip was arranged by the Nippo-Brazilian Cultural Institute, headquartered in the Japanese Embassy. Four other Brazilians were already studying in Japan under the institute's auspices, with all expenses reportedly paid by the Japanese Government.

subfiles.title: Quintuplicate copy of despatch on Brazilian cultural visitors to Japan
subfiles.from: R. M. Scotten, Counselor of Embassy, for the Ambassador
subfiles.about: This file copy duplicates the report on Japanese-funded university study by Brazilian cultural visitors.
subfiles.summary: The copy repeats that Aires de Azevedo would study Japanese literature in Tokyo under the sponsorship of the Nippo-Brazilian Cultural Institute. It names four earlier Brazilian participants and states that the Japanese Government paid the expenses. The final notation certifies it as a true copy of the signed original.

subfiles.title: Cross-reference sheet: Japanese Catholic mission to Brazil
subfiles.about: The sheet refers to a report on a Japanese Catholic goodwill mission headed by Admiral Shinjiro Yamamoto.
subfiles.summary: The note cross-references despatch No. 748 concerning the mission's visit to Rio de Janeiro. It calls the use of Japanese Catholics astute propaganda because Brazil was predominantly Catholic and the Church exercised strong moral influence.

subfiles.title: Consular despatch No. 280: Japanese Propaganda in Brazil
subfiles.from: M. L. Stafford, American Consul, Rio de Janeiro
subfiles.about: The despatch forwards a Japanese propaganda booklet supplied to the U.S. vice consul at Santos by the Japanese consul there.
subfiles.summary: Stafford transmits the English-language Japan-China Pictorial Primer: Do You Know That...?, published by the Japan Pacific Association to justify Japanese policy in China. Vice Consul Arthur G. Parsloe believed the Japanese consul at Santos had distributed it among prominent people in the district. Its number indicated that it belonged to a series of propaganda publications.

subfiles.title: Japan-China Pictorial Primer: Do You Know That...? No. 3
subfiles.about: The surviving portion of the booklet uses fifty rhetorical questions to justify Japan's war in China and criticize Chinese government, society, foreign relations, and resistance to Japan.
subfiles.summary: The booklet argues that foreign powers maintained troops, concessions, gunboats, customs officials, advisers, and other privileges in China, presenting Japan's position as comparable or more defensible. It depicts Chinese nationalism, boycotts, Communist influence, violence, military preparations, and Chiang Kai-shek's government as threats while emphasizing Japanese investments, alleged humanitarian conduct, cultural institutions, and economic dependence on China. Later pages defend Japanese control of Manchuria, describe Soviet influence in Outer Mongolia, and claim that population density, food dependence, immigration restrictions, and the need for industrial exports make expansion in the Chinese market vital. This section ends during question 45, so the booklet continues beyond page 80.
